cells.tense: What you received is changing in your hands right now, keeping its purpose and letting go of what it no longer needs.
cells.ask: Change one thing you carry forward so it fits the people in the room, say it once that way, and notice who receives it.
cells.core:
You hand things on and they come out alive. Much of what you carry is older than you, and you adjust it in the telling rather than repeating it exactly, because passing it on is the point rather than keeping it clean. People can tell when you do that. It reaches them, and they know they belong to something larger than the moment.

Maybe it is the way your family does a holiday, or how you explain something you learned, or how your team runs its work, and you are editing it a little to fit who is actually in front of you. That editing is the real skill, and the people you do it for rarely see it. Trust it, but keep an ear out: shaping a thing to the room can slide into telling people what they want. You can feel a room get whole — that is the moment to let the thing go.
cells.sheetLine: What you carry changes as you pass it on.
cells.place: where a shared thing is whole and can be let go

cells.tense: You are guarding a version of this against a future where someone gets it wrong, and the guard is hardening what you meant to keep.
cells.ask: Set the piece you protect hardest on the table this week, let whoever is there handle it their way, and treat how they handle it as the whole event.
cells.core:
You are defending a way of doing things, and the defense has stopped something. The version you are holding in place is the correct one, or the one that was handed to you, and anyone who does it differently is doing it wrong. Some of this is about the people who come after — you don't want it lost, so you hold loss away by making the form exact.

The exactness is draining the thing itself. People can sense when a tradition has become a standard, and they stop bringing themselves to it. This isn't about loosening everything. It's about finding the one place where the guard is harder than what it guards, and whether you can locate that spot. When you get the chance, put down the version and find out what the people around you already know how to do.
cells.sheetLine: You are keeping it so exact it has stopped being yours.
cells.place: where a shared thing is whole and can be let go

cells.tense: You put down what you were carrying a long time ago, and you have been starting over from nothing ever since.
cells.ask: Ask one person how they do the thing you do alone, and try their way once as more than a courtesy — run it even if it isn't yours.
cells.core:
You do things your own way, and you have for a while. Nothing gets handed to you and nothing gets handed on, so you work each thing out from the beginning, which is why you are good at it and also tired. Every result is a fresh one, and none of it connects to anything before it. That adds up to a lot of effort spent redoing what somebody already knew.

Maybe you started this because the way it was done didn't fit. Or because nobody sat you down and said here is how it's done. A thing passed from one person to another isn't a cage — somebody learned something that still holds, and it could reach you the same way, one person at a time, if you let it come in from outside. Ask for one piece that is already in someone else's hands.
cells.sheetLine: You've built from scratch so long, none of it connects to a line.
cells.place: where a shared thing is whole and can be let go

cells.tense: You keep showing up with what you know as if you were merely present, while people are already taking notes from what you do.
cells.ask: Name one thing you have been calling standard and say plainly, once, that you made it, to the person who follows it.
cells.core:
People copy how you work and what you say matters to them, and you describe it as if it happens on its own. You show up and hold a thing together for the people around you, and you call that just being there. The shaping is real. What is missing is your hand on it.

Look at the room after you have been in it: what changed, and was it you or was it luck? Once you see your own part there, you find out how much of the meaning around you rests on things you did and didn't think of as a decision. That is a smaller, earlier move than naming the whole thing — one item, plainly, owned to one person. No life story needed, just a sentence about a thing that came from you.
cells.sheetLine: This came from you, and people are following it.
cells.place: where a shared thing is whole and can be let go

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person hands something on in any deliberate form; the record shows transmission from what is shared, not that they claim it. A reader could say their gatherings are looser than the cell describes, or that they are passing nothing on at all. The asks still work if the read is wrong: none of them depends on being a teacher or on carrying a lineage. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'wisdom that can move' — it admires the formulation, so it goes.
